editor_note: Entry 91 is faithful and natural ("Mga Rekomendasyon", "i-extend ang Python gamit ang Qiskit C API", "Galugarin ang ... reference"). Entry 7 translates the "UNIX-like" section heading as "Katulad ng UNIX", but the rest of the page keeps the English term: entry 8 says "mga UNIX-like na sistema", and entries 27 and 80 send readers to "[UNIX-like](#unix) section" / "seksyong [UNIX-like](#unix)". A reader looking for that section finds a heading that doesn't match the name it was referred by. The meaning is correct and nobody is misled, but the heading should match the cross-references.

examples.why: Entries 8, 27 and 80 keep 'UNIX-like' in English, and 27 and 80 point readers to the '[UNIX-like]' section by name. The translated heading no longer matches those links. Keeping 'UNIX-like', as the body text already does, makes them match.

editor_note: The rewritten heading in entry 3 translates "Open source" half-way, as "Bukas na source". That is an awkward calque and not a term Filipino developers use. It also clashes with the rest of the page, where the page title (entry 1) keeps "Open source" and the body keeps "open-source" / "pag-open-source". The meaning still comes through, so nothing misleads, but the heading should go back to "Open source" to match.

examples.why: This half-translated calque mixes a Tagalog word with an English one and is not the standard term. It is also inconsistent with the title in entry 1 ('Open source') and the body text ('open-source na komunidad', 'pag-open-source'), which keep the English term the field uses.

editor_note: The meaning is faithful all the way through. Every IBM-versus-user split, including the "Hindi responsable ang IBM" backup rows, matches the English, so nothing here would mislead a learner. The main problem is "bawi" doing double duty. It stands for "revoking" access in [11]/[12] and for "recovery" in [5]/[17], so "Awtomatikong bawiin at ibalik ang mga kakayahan" in [17] can be misread as "automatically revoke and restore capabilities". Two smaller points: "recovery" appears as both "pagbawi" and the English "recovery" inside [5], and "in a transparent manner" became "nang malinaw" ("clearly") in [6]/[9], which loses the idea of open, visible delivery.

examples.source: Automatically recover and restore IBM Quantum Compute Service capabilities to normal operations.
examples.translation: Awtomatikong bawiin at ibalik ang mga kakayahan ng IBM Quantum Compute Service sa normal na operasyon.
examples.suggested: Awtomatikong i-recover at ibalik sa normal na operasyon ang mga kakayahan ng IBM Quantum Compute Service.
examples.why: 'bawiin' is also this file's word for revoking access ([11], [12]), so here it can read as 'withdraw the capabilities'. Using 'i-recover'/'ibalik' for recovery avoids that reading.

examples.source: problem determination, recovery, and full-state backup and recovery
examples.translation: pagtukoy ng problema, pagbawi, at buong backup at recovery
examples.suggested: pagtukoy ng problema, recovery, at full-state na backup at recovery
examples.why: 'Recovery' is rendered two ways in the same sentence. Also, 'buong backup' drops the 'full-state' nuance.

examples.source: Continuously deliver new features, updates, and bug fixes as needed in a transparent manner.
examples.translation: Patuloy na maghatid ng mga bagong feature, update, at bug fix ayon sa pangangailangan nang malinaw.
examples.suggested: ...ayon sa pangangailangan, sa paraang transparent/bukas sa mga user.
examples.why: 'nang malinaw' means 'clearly'. The English 'transparent' means openly visible to customers, so the nuance is flattened. The same thing happens in [9].

editor_note: Entry 27 "Teorema ng No-Cloning" is faithful to the English and uses natural Tagalog word order. It matches the file's own "Teorema" (figure title in [29]) and "teoremang ito" ([31]), and keeps "No-Cloning" as the recognizable term that the body uses in "no-cloning theorem".

Entry 8 (the fidelity definition) is faithful and does not need changes. "Hayaan ang $\rho$ at $\sigma$ na maging mga density matrix…" matches the "Hayaan … na maging" pattern used in entries 41 and 65, and "tinukoy gamit ang trace (Tr) bilang" is accurate. Entry 39 is the problem: the heading is fully translated as "Lemma ng Banayad na Pagsukat", but the paragraphs under it (entries 40, 44, 57) keep the name in English as *gentle measurement lemma*. So a learner sees two names for the same lemma, one in the heading and another in the text. The heading also uses Title Case, while the other headings on the page are sentence case ("Kahulugan ng fidelity", "Mga pangunahing katangian ng fidelity").

examples.why: The body text (entries 40, 44, 57) always calls it the English *gentle measurement lemma*, so the translated heading gives the same lemma a second name. The heading is also in Title Case, unlike the page's other sentence-case headings. Another fix is to keep the Tagalog heading and add the English name in the body: 'lemma ng banayad na pagsukat (*gentle measurement lemma*)'.

editor_note: Entry 11 (Credly notice) is faithful and complete, with every clause kept. Credly is described as "third-party na tagaproseso ng datos na awtorisado ng IBM", the hedge "Maaaring ibahagi ng IBM" preserves the English "may share", and "sa buong mundo" and "nang naaayon sa mga gawi ng IBM sa privacy" are both carried over intact.

Both rewritten entries keep the meaning and would not mislead a learner, but a native editor would change three small things. In entry 8, "hindi makilalang fermion" reads closer to "unrecognizable fermions" than "indistinguishable fermions" (particles that cannot be told apart). "hindi mapag-iba-ibang fermion" is more accurate and fits better with "magkaparehong fermion" in entry 12. Also in entry 8, the bare "Partikular," is a calque of "In particular"; "Sa partikular," or "Lalo na," sounds more natural. In entry 7, the singular "ito" refers back to the plural "mga Hamiltonian" and should be "ang mga ito".

examples.source: a fermionic Hamiltonian that governs indistinguishable fermions
examples.translation: namamahala sa mga hindi makilalang fermion
examples.suggested: namamahala sa mga hindi mapag-iba-ibang fermion
examples.why: 'hindi makilala' means unrecognizable/unknown. The physics concept is that the particles cannot be told apart, and the page already uses 'magkaparehong fermion' in entry 12.

examples.source: In particular, she describes the need for mapping
examples.why: A bare 'Partikular,' at the start of a sentence is a calque of the English connective. Tagalog uses 'Sa partikular,' or 'Lalo na,'.

examples.source: Hamiltonians and how to map them
examples.translation: sa mga Hamiltonian at kung paano ito ima-map
examples.suggested: sa mga Hamiltonian at kung paano ima-map ang mga ito
examples.why: The singular pronoun 'ito' does not agree with the plural 'mga Hamiltonian'.

editor_note: Both rewritten entries keep the meaning of the English and would not mislead anyone. Entry 9, "Iginawad na Badge", is fine. Entry 12 faithfully keeps every clause of the Credly privacy notice: the data shared (pangalan, email address, nakuhang badge), the US location, sharing "sa buong mundo", and the handling "naaayon sa mga privacy practice ng IBM". The one slip is "para sa mga layuning pag-uulat at operasyon ng programa". It has no linker ("layuning pag-uulat") and reads as a calque of "program reporting and operational purposes", so a native editor would recast it.

examples.source: Your personal information is used to issue your badge and for program reporting and operational purposes.
examples.translation: Ginagamit ang iyong personal na impormasyon upang ibigay ang iyong badge at para sa mga layuning pag-uulat at operasyon ng programa.
examples.suggested: Ginagamit ang iyong personal na impormasyon upang ibigay ang iyong badge, at para sa pag-uulat at mga layuning pang-operasyon ng programa.
examples.why: "mga layuning pag-uulat" has no linker (it should be "layunin ng pag-uulat" or "pang-uulat") and copies the English noun stack. The meaning is still clear.

editor_note: Both rewritten entries keep the English meaning, so neither would mislead a learner. Entry 50 ("Bilangin natin ang mga operasyon para sa circuit na ito.") reads naturally and needs no change. Entry 31 uses "pinapayagan nito tayong madaling pag-aralan", which copies English "allows us" as a word for giving permission. It also uses the plain verb "pag-aralan" where Tagalog grammar wants the "able to" form "mapag-aralan". A native technical editor would rephrase it as "nagbibigay-daan ito para madali nating mapag-aralan".

examples.source: This Hamiltonian is useful in that it allows us to easily study the effects of an external field.
examples.translation: Kapaki-pakinabang ang Hamiltonian na ito dahil pinapayagan nito tayong madaling pag-aralan ang mga epekto ng isang panlabas na field.
examples.suggested: Kapaki-pakinabang ang Hamiltonian na ito dahil nagbibigay-daan ito para madali nating mapag-aralan ang mga epekto ng isang panlabas na field.
examples.why: 'Pinapayagan' means giving permission, so it copies English 'allows' too literally. 'Pag-aralan' also needs the 'able to' form 'mapag-aralan' here. The meaning stays correct, but the sentence reads stiff.

editor_note: Entries 8 and 9 are faithful. The problem is entry 60: it renders the heading "Quantum Machine Learning" as the literal calque "Pag-aaral ng Makina sa Quantum", which reads more like "a machine's studying in quantum". The section body right below it (entry 61), and entry 48, keep "machine learning" in English, so the heading and body don't match. Entry 50 is accurate, but it translates "Problem-specific ansaetze" as "Mga ansaetze na partikular sa problema", while entries 51, 69 and 72 keep "problem-specific" in English, so the same term appears two ways. Neither issue would mislead a learner.

examples.why: This literal calque of "machine learning" is stiff and not how the field says it. It also clashes with the body text (entries 48 and 61), which keeps "machine learning" in English.

examples.translation: Mga ansaetze na partikular sa problema {#problem-specific-ansaetze}
examples.why: The translation is correct, but entries 51, 69 and 72 keep "problem-specific" in English. The summary bullet in entry 69 repeats this heading word for word, so the heading and the bullet read differently.

editor_note: None of the five rewritten entries would mislead a learner. Entries 74, 87 and 95 are faithful: "mag-o-optimize tayo", the orthogonality constraint and "naghihigpit sa search space" all match the English. The one problem is the bootstrap line, which appears twice with the same English and is translated two different ways. Entry 96 uses "Mag-bootstrap … kung mayroon kang" ("you"), though the English says "we". Entry 140 uses "I-bootstrap … kung mayroon tayong" ("we") but gives the verb no object. Both lines should use "Mag-bootstrap sa $i=0$ kung mayroon tayong katulad na problema".

examples.source: Bootstrap at $i=0$ if we have a similar problem (typically found via classical simulation or sampling).
examples.translation: Mag-bootstrap sa $i=0$ kung mayroon kang katulad na problema (karaniwang nahahanap sa pamamagitan ng klasikal na simulation o sampling).
examples.suggested: Mag-bootstrap sa $i=0$ kung mayroon tayong katulad na problema (karaniwang nahahanap sa pamamagitan ng klasikal na simulation o sampling).
examples.why: The source says 'we', and the translation switches it to 'you' (kang). Entry 140 translates the same sentence with 'tayo', so the two lines don't match.

examples.source: Bootstrap at $i=0$ if we have a similar problem (typically found by classical simulation or sampling).
examples.translation: I-bootstrap sa $i=0$ kung mayroon tayong katulad na problema (karaniwang nahahanap sa pamamagitan ng klasikal na simulation o sampling).
examples.suggested: Mag-bootstrap sa $i=0$ kung mayroon tayong katulad na problema (karaniwang nahahanap sa pamamagitan ng klasikal na simulation o sampling).
examples.why: 'I-bootstrap' puts the focus on an object, but the sentence has no object, so it reads awkwardly. It also differs from 'Mag-bootstrap' in entries 21, 64 and 96.

editor_note: None of the five rewritten entries would mislead a learner, but they make the page's terminology inconsistent. The rewritten headings translate the term fully ("Default na estado", "Klasikal na estado ng reperensiya", "Quantum na estado ng reperensiya", and in the summary list "Default na estado ng reperensiya"). The body and the untouched sibling entries 1, 17, 27-29 keep "reference state" / "default state" / "classical reference state" in English. So a heading and the paragraph under it now use different words for the same concept, and the summary list is split between the two styles. Entry 21 renders "Quantum machine learning" as "Pag-aaral ng makina sa quantum", a stiff calque of an established field name that Tagalog technical writing normally keeps as "Quantum machine learning".

examples.why: The body (entry 9) and summary (entry 27) say 'classical reference state'. The heading is the only place that uses the fully translated form, so the heading and its section name the concept differently. The same fix applies to entry 12 ('Quantum reference state') and entry 5 ('Default state', which entry 7 keeps as 'default state').

In the summary list, entries 27-29 say 'Mga classical/quantum/application-specific reference state'. Translating only this item breaks the parallel list, and the reader may think it names a different concept.

'Quantum machine learning' is an established field name, and the page keeps terms like VQC and feature map in English. The literal 'learning of a machine in quantum' reads as a stiff calque and does not work as a recognizable subfield name.
